name: Droplist
tagline: Hosted signup pages and email notifications for product drops and launch waitlists.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: A drop or waitlist tool is a form, a table of emails, a public page with a count, and a send button. None of those pieces are hard, and an agent can assemble all of them in an afternoon with a real database behind it. The only part you cannot code your way out of is email delivery, so you bolt on a transactional provider and live with their free tier. What you are actually paying for here is not the data model, it is the fact that someone else already made the page look good and already fought the spam bots. If you are running one launch and you own your list, self-hosting is fine.
coreLoopDIY: A public signup page that collects emails with double opt in, stores them locally, shows a live signup count and referral position, and lets you blast the list when a drop goes live.
requirements: a transactional email provider API key (Resend, Postmark, or SES)
a domain with SPF and DKIM records if you want the confirmation mails to land
somewhere to host that is not your laptop if the page needs to stay up during a launch
whatYouLose: Sender reputation: their emails land in inboxes, yours land in spam until you warm up a domain
Bot and disposable-email filtering that you will only notice is missing after a bot run
Templates and page polish that look intentional instead of like a form you wrote at midnight
Any integration with Shopify, Stripe, or an ESP that already holds your customers
Uptime during the exact ten minutes that actually matter
moatNotes: The moat is cosmetic plus deliverability, which is real but rentable from any email API.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a launch is a one-shot event with a hard deadline, and nobody wants their signup page to be the thing that breaks. Paying a small monthly fee buys a page that already converts, an inbox path that already works, and someone to blame at 9am. The build is easy; the confidence is what costs money. If you run drops continuously and the list is your asset, owning the stack starts making sense fast.
notes: Classic weekend-SaaS shape: trivial core, all the value sitting in polish and email plumbing.
prompt:
Build a self-hosted drop and waitlist signup app in an empty folder.

Stack, no substitutions: Next.js (App Router, TypeScript), Tailwind CSS, SQLite via better-sqlite3, Resend for email. No auth provider, no analytics, no telemetry.

What to build:
1. A public signup page at / with a headline, subhead, and an email field, all configurable in config.ts (product name, headline, drop date).
2. POST /api/subscribe: validate the email, reject disposable domains from a small hardcoded blocklist, rate limit by IP (10 per hour, in-memory is fine), insert as status=pending with a random confirm token and a referral code.
3. Send a confirmation email via Resend containing a link to /confirm?token=... which flips status to confirmed. Do not count pending signups publicly.
4. Show a live confirmed count and, after signup, the user's queue position plus their referral link (?ref=CODE). A referral that confirms moves the referrer up 5 places in the displayed position. Keep the real insert order immutable in the DB.
5. Admin at /admin behind a single password from ADMIN_PASSWORD in .env, checked server-side and stored in an httpOnly cookie. Admin shows the list, signup count over time as a plain table, a CSV export, and a compose box that sends one plaintext-plus-simple-HTML email to all confirmed subscribers in batches of 50 with a delay between batches.
6. Every email includes a working one-click unsubscribe link that sets status=unsubscribed. Never send to unsubscribed rows.

Out of scope: multiple campaigns, teams, payments, Shopify or Stripe integration, drag-and-drop email design, A/B tests.

Secrets in .env only: RESEND_API_KEY, FROM_EMAIL, ADMIN_PASSWORD, PUBLIC_BASE_URL. Ship a .env.example.
Create the SQLite schema in a migration script and seed nothing. Write a README with setup, how to run locally, and a blunt note that emails will go to spam until SPF and DKIM are configured on the sending domain.
